channel_name: This Week in Startups · Jason Calacanis
video_title: Airtable’s 80% off value crash: VCs explain why it’s still a win | E2321
gist: A VC roundtable (Jason Calacanis with Nico Bonatsos of Verdict Capital, Rick Heitzmann of FirstMark, and Aditya Agarwal of South Park Commons) dissects Bending Spoons' acquisition of Airtable at 2.7x ARR — a ~$2.25B equity value against an $11.7B peak — as the template for how 2021-vintage SaaS decacorns will actually exit. The panel then extends into codified secondary-selling policies now that IPOs are 15-30 years out, Robinhood's prediction-market revenue surge and its retail closed-end venture fund, and how open-source models and internal agent harnesses are restructuring both VC firms and seed-stage startups.

themes.theme: Airtable–Bending Spoons: anatomy of the SaaS down-exit

insights.claim: Bending Spoons acquired Airtable at roughly 2.7x ARR for about $2.25B in equity value, against a peak private valuation of $11.7B — roughly an 80% discount to the last mark.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Sets a live public comp for what 2021-vintage SaaS marks are actually worth on exit — roughly 2-3x ARR for a ~20%-growth asset, not the 50-70x forward multiples on the way in.
insights.quote: They just bought Air Table for 2.7 times a ARR. The company's price and valuation peaked at 11.7 billion. The current equity value on the deal was 2.25 billion.

insights.claim: Airtable's enterprise value in the Bending Spoons deal was only about $1.2B because roughly $1B of the $1.4B it had raised was still sitting on the balance sheet as cash.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The operating business was valued at ~3x the headline discount implies; unspent venture cash is what let late-stage investors get their money back and is a key variable when handicapping other zombie-unicorn exits.
insights.quote: Uh so obviously 80% discount that put the enterprise value at about 1.2 because they had apparently a billion dollars in cash. Uh they had raised 1.4 billion to date

insights.claim: Airtable was at roughly $400M+ ARR growing about 20% year-over-year at the time of the sale, which the panel argues makes ~$2.25B a defensible rather than a distressed price.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Reframes the 'crash' narrative: at 20% growth the multiple compression is arithmetic, not a company failure — the same math applies to dozens of other 2021 SaaS marks still carried at peak.
insights.quote: if you're at 400 million in ARR growing 20% having kind of raised 1.4 four billion. I mean, you know, in some ways, this is actually a reasonable price for the company.

insights.claim: Airtable's AI-first product was spun out of the company as a separate entity before the Bending Spoons transaction closed, leaving the legacy SaaS business to be sold.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A repeatable structure for stranded unicorns — sell the cash-flowing legacy asset to a consolidator, spin the AI effort into a clean cap table — and something to watch for in other down-round M&A.
insights.quote: There was also a wrinkle that the AI first product they were working on was spun out of the company before this deal was done.

insights.claim: Late-stage investors in Airtable got their capital back after about five years, validating the ZIRP-era thesis that the downside on a high-quality growth deal was par rather than a loss — but the same growth funds will lose money on that vintage overall.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Suggests 2021 growth-fund returns cluster around 1.0x with long duration — the real cost is time value and lost recycling, not nominal loss, which should compress LP appetite for that strategy.
insights.quote: No and that's what happened. The later stage investors got their money back in 5 years. Again not the end of the world but a lot of those growth funds are actually going to lose money from that time.

insights.claim: Private cap tables are structurally one-directional — engineered only to go up and to the right — which is why founders rarely have the courage to accept a mark-down exit even when it is the rational outcome.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: Explains why the backlog of stranded unicorns clears slowly and unpredictably: the constraint is cap-table mechanics and social pressure, not the availability of buyers.
insights.quote: private cap tables are only engineered to go uh up and to the right. they're not engineered to go down.

insights.claim: Rebuilding a stalled SaaS company inside its existing 'calcified' cap table fails because the team hired during the growth years is the wrong team to run a defensive, profitability-focused, PE-style shrink.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: Argues the consolidator's premium is organizational, not financial — expect more legacy SaaS to sell rather than self-restructure, feeding rollup acquirers' pipelines.
insights.quote: those are not the same of people that can basically over the next year or two would just need to slow down shrink play defense and try to optimize private equity style get the profitability up

insights.claim: The scarcest asset for founders and investors in stalled decacorns is time, not capital, and the correct move is to sell to a consolidator and recycle both into the current AI opportunity window.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Predicts an accelerating wave of down-exits over the next 2-3 years as boards optimize for time rather than headline valuation.
insights.quote: a lot of these companies which have become zombies, even if they were decacorns, you know, they're just chewing up people's time and hoping against hope. The right thing to do is move on.

themes.theme: Growth rate as venture's only variable

insights.claim: The only metric that determines venture outcomes is growth rate — not profitability, not cash-flow positivity — a lesson Aditya Agarwal says he learned early at Facebook.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Sets the underwriting hurdle: any 'efficient growth' pitch that trades growth for margin is structurally mispriced for a venture fund even if it is a good business.
insights.quote: the only thing that matters in our industry for venture kind of capital is growth rate. Like we nothing else matters. It's not profitability. It's not cash flow positive.

insights.claim: At peak 2021, SaaS companies were receiving term sheets within 24 hours at 50-70x forward revenue multiples, a level the panel now agrees was unsupportable absent sustained high growth.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Anchors the size of the multiple air-pocket still embedded in 2021-vintage private marks — the gap between 50-70x forward and 2.7x trailing is the write-down still to be recognized.
insights.quote: a lot of these SAS companies were essentially getting term sheets uh you know the classic kind of term sheets within 24 hours at 50 70x kind of forward multiples

insights.claim: Sustaining 45-50% annual growth for seven to eight years quadruples or quintuples revenue, but the gap between 40% and 20% growth is the difference between doubling every two years and every three-and-a-half to four — compounding works symmetrically against you on the way down.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Quantifies why a 20-point growth deceleration justifies an order-of-magnitude multiple compression, useful for stress-testing any high-multiple software position.
insights.quote: exponentials are beautiful on the way up, they kind of kill you on the way down as well.

insights.claim: A Series A or B investor must underwrite roughly 100x from entry for the venture math to work at the fund level, which is why anything below hypergrowth is punished so severely.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Explains the structural pressure on early investors to push portfolio companies toward risk rather than durability — and why consolidators can buy those assets cheaply.
insights.quote: even if you kind of look at somebody who came in at the series A or series B, what you're really underwriting is kind of 100x from there, right? To kind of like make the venture math work out

themes.theme: Software rollups as the emerging exit venue

insights.claim: Bending Spoons' operating playbook on acquired assets is to cut roughly 80% of staff, install young leadership, and run the products AI-first for profitability — the model it applied to AOL and Meetup.com.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Defines the acquirer's margin thesis: AI-driven cost takeout is what makes an 80%-off SaaS asset accretive, and a template competitors will copy.
insights.quote: cut 80% of the staff, put young people in charge of these products or services from what I understand, and run them AI first for profitability.

insights.claim: Bending Spoons trades around a $30B market cap and is up about 40% from its IPO, which it executed the week after SpaceX went public despite fears that SpaceX would absorb all IPO demand.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A ~$2.25B acquisition is only 3-4% of market cap, meaning Bending Spoons can absorb many more of these deals — and the post-SpaceX trading proves the IPO window is wider than feared.
insights.quote: But even Bending Spoons is up 40% from its IPO. And then they they also had the courage to go public a week after SpaceX when everyone was afraid that SpaceX would s would take all the oxygen out of the room

insights.claim: Constellation Software has run the same acquisition model for nearly 30 years — buy at roughly 1x revenue, raise prices, remove employees — and compounded roughly 100x as a public company since around 2000.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Establishes the long-run public-market proof for the software-rollup model and a valuation benchmark (1x revenue) that competes directly with venture exit expectations.
insights.quote: hey we'll pay one times revenue we'll crank up pricing we'll take out the employees and if you look at it it's a public company it's really compounded over the last 20 years

insights.claim: Rollup acquirers have raised prices 100-200% at acquired software companies — the specific action venture-backed boards are unwilling to take themselves.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Identifies the arbitrage: latent pricing power in mature SaaS that venture governance suppresses, which is the true source of the consolidator's return.
insights.quote: part of the model is we're willing to do the hard things that maybe your VC board members wouldn't do. We're willing to make the cuts, implement AI, and increase prices.

insights.claim: Thrive Capital and General Catalyst are running verticalized AI rollups — the accounting sector is one target — which is the same model with more financial engineering than a traditional venture firm would attempt.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Signals venture capital itself migrating toward PE-style buyout structures, blurring the asset-class line and creating a new bid for legacy services businesses.

themes.theme: Secondaries and the shift from TVPI to DPI

insights.claim: The number of public companies in America has fallen roughly 20% over the last decade because companies increasingly don't want to be public, forcing venture firms to source liquidity privately.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Structural driver behind the secondary-market boom; any fund model assuming IPO exits inside a 10-year life is mispriced.
insights.quote: the number of public companies in America has gone down by 20% in the last decade people don't want to be public it kind of sucks to be a public company

insights.claim: Time-to-IPO has stretched from about four years in the 1990s, to a 5-7 year underwriting assumption around 2009-2010, to 20+ years for SpaceX and potentially 50 years or never for Stripe.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: Fund lives of 10-15 years can no longer contain hold periods, mechanically forcing GPs to become active sellers regardless of philosophy.
insights.quote: when I started in venture capital in 2009 2010 we were underwriting okay you know these companies could go public in like 5 to seven years and now many companies won't go public until like you know in this case of SpaceX 20 plus years later

insights.claim: South Park Commons runs a formulaic secondary rule — in a company-sanctioned sale, if selling roughly 15-20% of its position returns half a turn to a full turn of DPI, it sells — deliberately avoiding case-by-case price discovery with brokers.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: A concrete, copyable liquidity policy; also a signal that seed funds are systematically supplying secondary paper into later rounds.
insights.quote: if the sale is happening it's sanctioned by the company if I can sell 20% of my position return kind of like 0.5x kind of DPI to my LPs I'm going to do it

insights.claim: South Park Commons raised a $575M Fund IV, a step up from roughly $270M in Fund III, and attributes LP enthusiasm specifically to having demonstrated realized returns rather than paper markups.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Direct evidence that DPI, not TVPI, is now the binding constraint on emerging-manager fundraising — a filter to apply to any GP pitch.
insights.quote: fund four we just launched it 575 million meaningful step up from fund three which was about 270 and I think a big part of the reason why LPs were excited about kind of fund four is because we had shown TPI for fund one

insights.claim: Verdict Capital trims 5-10% of its position on the way up each time it evaluates a large round, especially when sitting on ~100x TVPI or when founders themselves are selling $20-50M, arguing this also creates a market for the next round.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: A first-money-in fund openly systematizing partial exits — a behavior change that adds persistent secondary supply and dampens the late-stage bid.
insights.quote: we trim 5 to 10% on the way up because in this big rounds normally here's what happens there going to be people who either didn't hear about it or missed out or lost the opportunity who two months later are gonna be so freaking you know hungry to get in.

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis pares 10-20% of a position at 50x and another 10-20% at 100-200x, and cites clearing an $18M position in a SaaS company that had hit $1B and is now likely worth under $100M.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A concrete case where mechanical trimming captured a 10x+ better outcome than holding — the strongest argument in the episode for pre-committed sell rules.
insights.quote: Did it with a SAS company that hit a billion that's probably now worth less than hundred million. Cleared $18 million position was one of the best you know distributions we ever had as a firm.

insights.claim: Contractual pro-rata sale rights alongside founders let an investor sell over founder objection, and framing it as an obligation to LPs plus an identical pari passu treatment is what makes it survivable relationally.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A negotiating template for early investors: secure tag-along rights at entry, then use symmetry with the founder as the social cover to exercise them.
insights.quote: We have a contractual right to sell alongside you and we have a contractual obligations to our LPs who we told we would do that. So if you guys are selling, we're selling. If you're not selling, we're not selling.

insights.claim: The majority of secondary brokers and SPV peddlers are characterized as boiler-room operators, and founders are right to object to unknown parties appearing indirectly on their cap tables.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Counterparty risk in private secondaries is being flagged by the practitioners themselves — a caution for anyone buying private exposure through intermediated vehicles.
insights.quote: the brokers in some cases are complete utter boiler room scumbags. I'll just say it outright.

insights.claim: Late-stage private rounds are now used to transition cap tables the way IPOs used to — swapping seed funds out for Wellington, Fidelity, or BlackRock who intend to add on at the IPO.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Reframes pre-IPO crossover rounds as book-building exercises; the identity of late private buyers becomes a leading indicator of IPO demand.
insights.quote: you might rather have more Wellington, more Fidelity, more long-term public capital on your cap table than a seed fund who, you know, is going to be up 100x in the IPO and is holding their breath till the lockup

insights.claim: Founder secondary sales in the last three to four years have been far smaller than the headline cases suggest — typically a couple million dollars for a house down payment rather than the $200M outlier at a conferencing software company.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Pushes back on the 'founders got rich and quit' narrative; the motivation-risk concern applies to a narrow set of 2020-2021 deals, not the current cohort.
insights.quote: this is what Mark did for us at Facebook in 2007 when we had our first secondary sale everybody was allowed to kind of do about like a million or two in secondary and it allowed basically all of us who are early employees to buy a house

themes.theme: Prediction markets and retail access to private assets

insights.claim: Robinhood's prediction-market business, launched in March 2025, generated $156M in Q2 revenue versus $342M for options, making event contracts its second-largest business line ahead of stock trading.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A roughly 15-month ramp to a nine-figure quarterly line item — the clearest hard number on how fast event contracts are monetizing for a retail brokerage.
insights.quote: options made 342 million in revenue in Q2. Event contracts prediction markets made 156 million.

insights.claim: Robinhood still relies on Kalshi for the underlying technology powering its prediction markets, meaning the infrastructure layer is concentrated in a third party.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Kalshi captures economics across multiple distribution front-ends; a picks-and-shovels position in the prediction-market boom rather than a pure competitor to Robinhood.
insights.quote: Robin Hood though uh still relies on Kouchy for its underlying technology.

insights.claim: Federal futures-contract structure, rather than state-by-state gaming licenses, is what unlocked the prediction-market category, though state AGs are now pushing back.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: The regulatory arbitrage is the whole business model — AG action is the single biggest tail risk to the revenue ramp at Robinhood, Kalshi, and Polymarket.
insights.quote: part of it was the opening up of the futures contracts instead of having to go state by state for a regulatory basis. that's opened up tremendously. Some of that's being pulled back by the AGs today

insights.claim: Prediction markets are heading into the same wallet-share war that sports betting fought five years ago, with DraftKings, FanDuel, Fanatics, Polymarket, Kalshi and Robinhood all competing for the same largely young-male demographic.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Implies a coming collapse in take rates and a spike in customer-acquisition spend — margin compression should be priced into any prediction-market exposure.
insights.quote: So, you're going to see that same battle for the customer wallets that you saw originally in the sports betting world from about 5 years ago.

insights.claim: Robinhood Ventures Fund 2 is targeting a $200-230M NYSE listing on August 13 as a publicly traded closed-end fund that gives non-accredited retail investors exposure to private companies, already holds stakes in 80 startups, and charges a 2% management fee.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: A new permanent-capital vehicle bidding for the same seed-stage assets traditional VCs buy, with an explicit YC focus — direct competition for allocation at the earliest stage.
insights.quote: They're targeting 200 million in the IPO New York Stock Exchange August 13th.

insights.claim: Founders resist retail closed-end fund vehicles because they lose control over who ends up on their cap table — illustrated by the AngelList USVC / Anduril dispute in which Brian Schimpf publicly objected.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Cap-table access, not capital, is the binding constraint on retail-private products — a structural limit on how large these vehicles can get in the best companies.
insights.quote: it kind of makes essentially founders feel like they're not in complete control of their cap table

insights.claim: A prior Robinhood-linked vehicle holding Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX debuted strongly and traded up, but a retail fund buying a slate of YC seed financings is a much weaker proposition because those assets lack understandable models.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Suggests retail private-market vehicles will price well only for late-stage brand-name assets and could trade at steep discounts when stuffed with seed-stage paper.
insights.quote: I'm not sure having them invest in a slate financing at YC makes any sense.

insights.claim: Many LP agreements prohibit exposure to vice categories — gambling, adult content, psychedelics — which structurally limits which funds can back emerging categories like prediction markets and creates less-contested entry for those who can.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: An identifiable capital-supply gap: categories excluded by LP mandates get funded at lower valuations by the few firms with carveouts.
insights.quote: a lot of our LP packs our agreements with LPs don't allow us to go into vice gambling

insights.claim: Backing regulatorily contested categories requires pre-committing to LPs on where you will and won't operate and then holding conviction when regulators attack — the pattern FirstMark followed with DraftKings, Airbnb and Uber, and earlier faced with Riot Games over its name.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: A reusable template for underwriting gray-area categories: define the legal perimeter up front with LPs so the inevitable regulatory shock doesn't force a forced sale.
insights.quote: We're starting in daily fantasy and we'll only participate in the markets in states where this is legal. We're not going to play in the gray area.

insights.claim: South Park Commons backed an AI forecasting company that claims to beat the best human superforecasters on prediction-market questions, and one of its founders turned $35 into nearly $2 million on Kalshi using it.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: If AI forecasters systematically beat human traders, retail-facing prediction markets face an adverse-selection problem that could compress liquidity and spreads.
insights.quote: one of the founders turned 35 bucks into almost $2 million on Cali just kind of like using this

themes.theme: Open-source models and AI inside the VC firm

insights.claim: A single user query to OpenEvidence fans out into roughly 50 separate model calls, and 80-90% of those calls go to open-source models rather than frontier APIs.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: The most concrete datapoint in the episode on frontier-lab revenue risk: production AI apps are already routing the overwhelming majority of inference to open weights.
insights.quote: right now like 80 to 90% of the calls to uh within that open evidence kind of one call trace happens to open source models.

insights.claim: South Park Commons employs six to seven engineers out of a 30-person firm — roughly 20% of headcount — building its own internal agent harness, having abandoned Hermes after catastrophic memory loss.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Venture firms are becoming software companies; the off-the-shelf agent-harness layer is not yet reliable enough for firms that can afford to build, which is a product gap.
insights.quote: We started off using Hermes but then that you know ended up kind of having like catastrophic memory loss. Uh but nowadays we we built our own harness. We actually multiplex between different models.

insights.claim: South Park Commons went from about 100 total commits in its firm's entire history as of February to 5,000 commits five months later, with all GPs committing code almost daily.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: A 50x internal-tooling output jump in five months is a measurable proxy for the leverage AI coding tools deliver to non-engineering organizations.
insights.quote: As of this February, in our code base, we had about a 100 commits in the history of our firm. Five months later, we have 5,000.

insights.claim: Every South Park Commons employee has a personal AI agent and nobody has an executive assistant, and Kimi is currently the firm's preferred open-source model for long-horizon tasks.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Executive-assistant headcount is an early, visible casualty of agent adoption; and a Chinese open-weight model winning a US fund's default slot is a real competitive datapoint.
insights.quote: Our favorite open source model right now is Kimmy.

insights.claim: South Park Commons absorbed 50% year-over-year growth in applications with no headcount increase and now gives personalized feedback to rejected applicants despite a 1% acceptance rate, purely through AI tooling.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Concrete demonstration that AI decouples throughput from headcount in a relationship business — the same logic applies to any high-volume screening operation.
insights.quote: our curve has essentially increased 50% year-over-year. Our firm hasn't increased by 50% year-over-year. We're still the same size.

insights.claim: FirstMark builds a per-deal AI project aggregating every meeting transcript, deck and prior analysis, so partners enter investment reviews with 10-20x more knowledge and the process optimizes for truth rather than for an answer.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: Points at a defensible workflow: proprietary meeting-transcript corpora become the firm's real asset, raising the value of note-capture tooling across professional services.
insights.quote: our purpose of our investment process is getting to truth and as opposed to getting to an answer. And this helps us get to truth in a in a lot more transparent way.

insights.claim: South Park Commons is backing Goodfire, an AI interpretability lab that just released a product letting users inspect which model weights activated and why a model pursued a given line of reasoning, positioned against long-horizon cybersecurity agent tasks.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Interpretability is being commercialized as an enterprise requirement for autonomous agents, not just a safety research field — a fundable category.
insights.quote: GoodFire is kind of the leading uh AI interpretability lab. And what that really means is that you can go and introspect what is happening in these models. It's no longer has to be a black box.

themes.theme: What a fundable founder looks like now

insights.claim: South Park Commons deliberately avoids companies whose only advantage is code that can be vibe-coded, and prefers founders whose edge is domain depth in semiconductors, nuclear fusion, autonomous ships, or grid infrastructure where code is an accelerant rather than the moat.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Signals capital rotating away from thin AI application wrappers toward deep-tech and physical-AI where LLMs compress execution but don't erase the barrier.
insights.quote: if your only kind of alpha is in some ways spinning up a code to solve I think what would feel like a more contained business problem I think we tend to shy away from those.

insights.claim: A strong founding team with AI tools plus one round of funding and two months of work can now reach what previously took two rounds, ten people, and a full year — effectively letting a company skip three rounds of progress.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: Compresses the seed-to-Series-A milestone ladder, which should push entry valuations up while shrinking dollars-in per milestone.
insights.quote: It means that you raise one round of funding and you can basically skip to like three rounds later if you're indeed you know those kind of freaks.

insights.claim: Lower barriers to starting a company have flooded the funnel with grifters and status-seekers, so the diagnostic has shifted from 'can they build it' to 'will they persist' — because anybody can now get a few customers.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: Predicts a rising seed-stage failure rate and a shift in selection criteria toward durability signals, which is where mispricing will concentrate.
insights.quote: It's like actually I I'm trying to figure out if people are going to quit. Will they stick with this? because anybody can get a couple of customers now.

insights.claim: With time, the diagnostic is slope — whether the pitch and output visibly improve between meetings days apart; without time, the fallback is asking a founder seven times why they are building what they are building until they run out of content.
insights.speaker: Nico Bonatsos
insights.so_what: A compressed-diligence heuristic for an environment where deals close in days rather than weeks.
insights.quote: If you don't have the benefit of time, just go back old school. Ask them seven times why they're building what they're building. And if they run out of content, probably you know your answer.

insights.claim: Rick Heitzmann endorses Paul Graham's observation that email response speed and thoughtfulness is a reliable founder signal, because it indicates the founder is on top of their business and competitive landscape.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: A cheap, testable screen usable inside a single diligence cycle — particularly valuable now that product traction is a weaker differentiator.
insights.quote: how fast do people respond to emails a as just a data point

insights.claim: Jason Calacanis argues remote work fails for roughly 80% of people and doesn't create a hard-driving culture, treating the 2020-2022 forced-remote period as a contributing cause of stalled growth at that vintage.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: If widely held among allocators, this becomes a diligence criterion that disadvantages distributed-first companies in fundraising.
insights.quote: we all know like remote work just doesn't work for 80% of people and it doesn't create the proper hard driving culture

insights.claim: FirstMark invested in Overtone Networks, founded by Hinge founder Justin McLeod, building an audio-first conversational AI matchmaker — with audio-first interaction called out as a coming trend in consumer AI applications.
insights.speaker: Rick Heitzmann
insights.so_what: A named bet that the consumer application layer, differentiated on UX and audio interface rather than model quality, is where the next generation of consumer value accrues.
insights.quote: They're also being which I think is going to be a trend in AI and LLM of being audio first.

themes.theme: Talent mobility, IP, and the Apple–OpenAI fight

insights.claim: The burden of evidence in the Apple–OpenAI talent dispute sits with Apple, since in decades of funding people leaving large companies the panel has almost never seen a trade secret actually used to build a competitive product.
insights.speaker: Aditya Agarwal
insights.so_what: Suggests such suits are reputational maneuvers rather than existential threats — unlikely to slow the flow of hardware talent into AI startups.
insights.quote: the onus, the burden of evidence here is really on Apple to prove that something wrong happened cuz in all my years of funding people who have left companies, I have almost never seen somebody taking a trade secret

insights.claim: The operative rule for departing employees is that whatever is in your brain can leave with you but whatever is on your laptop, in your notes, or in a meeting-transcript tool cannot.
insights.speaker: Jason Calacanis
insights.so_what: The proliferation of AI meeting recorders creates a new category of portable-but-prohibited artifact — a live compliance risk for any founder spinning out of a large employer.
insights.quote: Whatever's on your laptop or in your notes does not come with you. So if you kept a moles skin in of all your meetings or a granola of all your meetings or whatever transcript don't

insights.claim: US enforcement norms around IP agreements are themselves a competitive advantage over jurisdictions where source code is simply copy-pasted, and eroding that norm would be self-destructive.
